newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Wheat Board seeks high credit rating.
newsitem.headline: Australian Wheat Board seeks high credit rating.

text.p: The Australian Wheat Board (AWB), which raises up to A$4 billion a year in international borrowings, is aiming to achieve a credit rating of "A" or better after loss of Australian government guarantees on its debt in July 1999, AWB deputy chairman Robert Barry said.

Barry told an AWB in-house conference that the bulk of the A$550 million capital base the AWB was accumulating through grower levies would be mainly used to support wheat pool arrangements under which the board acquired growers' wheat at a guaranteed price before the wheat was internationally sold.

Benefits of existing government debt backing were that the government guaranteed payment of 85 percent of pool prices to growers, as well as allowing the AWB the same international credit rating as that of the Australian government, he said.
Australia's long term foreign debt is currently rated AA2 by Moody's Investors Service and AA by Standard and Poors.
The government guarantee provided a very significant benefit to the AWB in terms of cost as well as in ensuring the AWB access to capital markets, Barry said.
About half the AWB's post-1999 capital would be required to guarantee the minimum 85 percent payment to growers, Barry said.

However, the AWB also would be assuming significant risks in terms of paying growers when the wheat had not yet been sold as well as in guaranteeing Australian dollar prices when most of the wheat was sold in U.S. dollars, he said.
This put the AWB in a "risky, volatile" business where its earnings could be affected from year-to-year, he said.

The balance of the capital would give the AWB a debt/equity ratio which would ensure a credit rating of "A" or better, he said. This would occur through a gearing ratio of about 50 percent, Barry said.

While capital would be used to guarantee a minimum price to growers, the post-1999 AWB may not be able to pay a full price up-front in big-crop years -- payments in some years may have to be staggered, he said.

Barry also said that in his view the financing functions of the AWB -- payments to growers and supporting debt-raising -- should be contestable by banks and financial institutions in the open market. However, he said the AWB's marketing function through its single desk monopoly on exports should not be.
The AWB's financial advisers had suggested the AWB should receive a rate of 15 percent return on its capital, Barry said.
If the AWB were simply marketing wheat it would not need such a large capital base, he said.
But he said the industry wanted a guaranteed price as well as payments in advance of international sales.
The AWB is moving toward listing on the Australian Stock Exchange after 1999, although there is yet little agreement in the industry on its financial organisation after de-regulation.
